newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Maverick Serb generals meet rival politicians.
newsitem.headline: Maverick Serb generals meet rival politicians.

text.p: Ousted Bosnian Serb generals met their political leaders on Monday after weekend talks failed to resolve a dispute over who is to run the army.
Two days of discussions between Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic and top generals ended inconclusively on Saturday.
The standoff stems from Plavsic's decision to sack commander General Ratko Mladic and other top generals a week ago -- a move the army has so far refused to recognise.
Top generals, except for Mladic and his closest aide, General Milan Gvero, met Plavsic in Banja Luka on Monday and one senior commander hinted that a resolution may be imminent.
"There is always a solution to any problem. We are seeing one now," he said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Plavsic was meeting generals Momir Talic, Novica Simic, Zdravko Tolimir, Zivomir Ninkovic and former chief of staff Manojlo Milovanovic. Sources said the newly appointed commander, General Pero Colic, might attend the meeting.
The two sides traded insults over the weekend, with Colic accusing the sacked officers of clinging to their jobs out of ambition.
"This crisis is a crisis of individuals, sickly ambitious people," Bosnian Serb television quoted Colic as saying.
"All they see is the loss of their own positions and that is why they -- like all people who are not up to serious jobs -- can harm both themselves and others," he said.
Bosnian Serb media, under the control of civilian authorities, also reported that army officers had taken control of a TV transmitter on Mount Zep in eastern Bosnia last Tuesday.
The seizure prevented Serb television, based in the government seat Pale, from broadcasting to other towns in Bosnia's Serb republic.
Bosnian Serb civilian authorities ruled out resorting to violence but said they "must contemplate whether to take some of these so-called officers to court".
There was no response to this from Bosnian Serb army headquarters in the northeastern village of Han Pijesak.
The mood was tense in Han Pijesak, which served as the army's base during 3-1/2 years of war in Bosnia.
Milovanovic lashed out at the civilian authorities in a Belgrade newspaper interview.
"The conflict between the Interior Ministry and the army of the (Bosnian) Serb republic is on the brink of an open conflict and threatens to become a genuine civil war," he said.
Serb generals loyal to Mladic, an indicted war criminal who must step down under the Dayton peace agreement, insist the general staff should have a say over who will succeed him.
They scoff at newly-appointed commanders as unqualified party hacks.
Officers in the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia were following the standoff closely but declined to comment.
Diplomats say the West would be glad to see Mladic go but fears the peace process could be damaged if the power struggle drags on.
